lesson_title: Exponential Form of Whole Numbers and Integers
hook_text: Fold it five times. Thirty-two layers. Fold it ten — you can't.
clip_script: Take a sheet of paper and fold it in half. One fold, two layers. Fold again: four layers. Again: eight. The number of layers after each fold is a power of two — two to the power of the number of folds. After five folds you have two to the power five, thirty-two layers, and the stack is already hard to fold. After ten folds you would have two to the power ten, one thousand and twenty-four layers, thicker than a book. Nobody manages more than seven or eight folds with ordinary paper, and this is why: the layers do not grow by adding two each time, they double, and doubling runs away from you.
visual_style: A sheet of paper folding in half repeatedly with the layer count ticking up as a power of two; the stack thickening until it jams
pacing: quick folds, a pause at thirty-two
call_to_action: Open the full session to master powers of integers and the bracket rule.
